t: Kraków grew from a fortified settlement of the Vistulans on Wawel Hill into the seat of the Polish government from 1038 and the capital of the kingdom until Sigismund III Vasa moved his court to Warsaw in 1596.

The city was sacked by the Mongols in 1241, rebuilt from 1257 with Magdeburg rights, and gained the university founded by Casimir III in 1364, which became a centre of Polish learning and art under the Jagiellonian kings.

After the partitions it passed to Habsburg rule, became a Polish national and cultural centre under Austrian Galicia, and was the capital of the General Government in the Second World War, when its large Jewish population was confined in a ghetto and murdered.
dyk: The so-called dragon bones displayed at the entrance of Wawel Cathedral, tied to the legend of the dragon of Wawel Hill, are most likely those of a mammoth.

f.founded: Around the 8th century, as a fortified settlement of the Vistulans, a Lechitic tribe; a legend attributes the founding to the mythical ruler Krakus.
f.where: On the Vistula river in the Lesser Poland region of southern Poland, about 219 metres above sea level, at the meeting of the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland, the Małopolska Upland, the Sandomierz Basin and the foothills of the Carpathians.
f.known: Wawel Hill with its castle and cathedral; the seat of the Piast and Jagiellonian kings; the Jagiellonian University of 1364; the Main Market Square and St Mary's Basilica; the Jewish quarter of Kazimierz; the Kraków Ghetto; Karol Wojtyła, who became Pope John Paul II
f.today: Kraków is the second-largest city of Poland and the capital of the Lesser Poland Voivodeship, and its Old Town is a World Heritage Site.
